title: Enmity ends at death
hookLine: after Mandodari's grief, a funeral, a coronation, and two acts of mercy
last: MASTERING THE SENSES IS NEVER DONE ONCE.

lines: A KING STILL ON THE FIELD.
cards: Mandodari's lament ends. The other women lift her gently and lead her back toward the city. Ravana's body still lies on the field.
Someone has to perform his funeral rites, and by custom that duty falls to his closest kin: Vibhishana. But Vibhishana stands back. He tells Rama he can't do it.
This man was cruel, he says, he wronged others' wives, he was against everything right. How can I honor him?

teach.b: Rama's answer is short, and it is still quoted. Enmity ends at death. Our purpose is finished.

teach.h: HE IS MINE AS MUCH AS YOURS.
teach.b: He is mine now, as much as he is yours. Think about who's saying this: the man whose wife Ravana stole, whose brother Ravana nearly killed. The moment the war is over, Rama refuses to carry the hatred one step further.
Ravana was a great warrior, he says, and deserves a king's funeral. So Vibhishana does it, with fire and ritual, as a brother.
These last rites, antyeshti, are the final rite of passage of a Hindu life, and Rama won't let even his enemy be denied them. Mandodari saw Ravana whole; Rama lets him be honored whole.
Then Rama has Vibhishana crowned king of Lanka, properly this time, and sends Hanuman into the city with the news for Sita. There a second mercy waits.

Hanuman finds Sita in the grove, surrounded by the rakshasi guards who threatened her for months. He tells her Ravana is dead, and she's too moved to speak. Then he offers, angrily, to kill every one of the guards.
Sita stops him. They were servants following a king's orders, she says. And then, in Valmiki, she says something that sounds like a whole teaching.
A noble person shows compassion to the guilty and the good alike, because no one is without fault.
Two people with every reason for revenge, Rama and Sita, on the same day, both refuse it.

how: Rama's words that enmity ends at death (maraṇāntāni vairāṇi) and Sita's mercy toward her guards are quoted by Hindu teachers on forgiveness and on treating the dead with respect.

o: Ravana's queen, whose grief gives way to his funeral rites

games.q: after the war — tap the pairs.

s: Rama forbids a funeral for Ravana
he tells Vibhishana to give him full rites: he is mine as much as yours.
Sita asks Hanuman to spare her rakshasi guards
she says they followed orders, and no one is without fault.
Vibhishana is eager to honor his brother
at first he refuses, because of Ravana's cruelty; Rama persuades him.

games.q: you're Sita. Ravana is dead, and Hanuman offers to kill the guards who threatened you for months. what do you say?
games.why: she spares them: they followed a king's orders, and a noble person shows compassion because no one is without fault.

practice: Bring to mind an old conflict that is truly over, a job you left or a fight from years ago, and notice whether some anger still rides along.
You don't have to forgive anything now; just try Rama's sentence quietly, it's over, and set one ounce of it down on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Mandodari. After her lament, Ravana is given a king's funeral by Rama's command, and Sita refuses revenge on the guards who tormented her.

orig.note: Sanskrit maraṇāntāni vairāṇi: enmities end at death; Rama's words to Vibhishana.

carryVoice: Your line: enmity ends at death. Ahead is the reunion Sita has waited for. Day six hundred fifty-seven.
